# Abstract

Personal vehicle ownership is a major financial burden for American households. Sprawling  metropolitan urban planning makes car ownership mandatory to access employment, healthcare and essential services exacerbating inequality and financial burden for poor households. This study examines the relationship between transit equity, built environment characteristic and accessibility  across Douglas and Sarpy county in Nebraska and Pottawattamie county in Iowa. Using the Using the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency’s Smart Location Database (SLD 3.0) we apply a multi-method approach to investigate automobile dependence and transit accessibility across the Omaha council bluffs metropolitan region. Clustering results showed spatial differences in the degree of automobile dependence. Neighborhoods in the urban core exhibit lower automobile ownership while peripheral neighborhoods had lower transit access and higher automobile ownership. Predictive modeling identifies that residential density and physical stop contribute the most to automobile dependence. Spatial accessibility analysis identified transit deserts located in the central Omaha as well as car-free block groups experiencing  employment accessibility deficits. Finally  nonparametric testing reveal a transit disparity along the state border with Council Bluffs residents experiencing lower access to transit and employment opportunity. These findings help urban planners identify where best to target transit investments to reduce automobile dependence.
